newsitem.title: INDIA: India rupee overvalued by REER terms--RBI.
newsitem.headline: India rupee overvalued by REER terms--RBI.

text.p: India's rupee appears to be overvalued according in the light of an analysis of Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) data, a senior official of the country's central bank said on Friday.

"There is a considerable discussion as to whether the rupee is overvalued or not," Deputy Governor Y.V. Reddy of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) told a meeting of forex dealers in the Indian resort state of Goa.

"As per the REER it would certainly appear so, irrespective of the base chosen," Reddy added. "The overvaluation has got exacerbated with the sharp appreciation of the US dollar against the other major currencies -- the Deutsche mark and the yen."
For most of 1996, Reddy said, the REER was stable. But the rupee appreciated in real terms from the last quarter of 1996 onwards as the dollar rose sharply vis-a-vis the other major currencies.
Last April, the trade-based REER (1985=100) rose to 65.41, an appreciation of about five percent over the August 1996 figure of 62.26. Over January 1996, the appreciation in April was 10.3 percent.

Reddy said the relative "cheapening" of imports may not have resulted in increasing imports and larger currrent account deficits, because imports are relatively less responsive to exchange rate changes and are more sensitive to the level of economic activity.

"There could be a potential larger current account deficit as industrial activity rebounds -- even at the present exchange rates and if oil demand picks up, a correction cannot be ruled out," Reddy added.
Global investment bank Merrill Lynch said in its August India report that the strong rupee was hurting Indian exports.

"Exports grew at only four percent in FY 1996/97 (April-March) against an 18 percent average growth rate for the previous three years," Merrill's report said. "The real appreciation of the rupee is having a negative impact on exports."
The rupee has remained steady at 35.70/80 against the dollar for the past one year.
